Each distractor rests on a different mistake about how the doctrine operates.

questions.learningObjective: apply the doctrine of reasoning by analogy and distinction to a concrete legal fact pattern
questions.stem: The record: A judge comparing two disputes extends a rule to a new setting. The earlier rule had a clear rationale. Which account of the governing rule is faithful to the doctrine?

options.text: Cases are analogous whenever the judge wants them to come out the same way on these facts.
An analogy is strong when the similarities between the cases are the ones that matter to the rule's rationale, not merely superficial facts on these facts.
Two cases are automatically analogous if they share one visible fact on these facts.
Courts may never extend a rule by analogy because that would create new law on these facts.

questions.explanation: Analogical reasoning depends on relevance. The advocate must show that the features shared by the cases are the features that explain the earlier result, so treating them alike is justified by the rule itself. Here the decisive point is reasoning from material similarities, so the result follows from that doctrine rather than from the surface appeal of a competing statement. Each distractor rests on a different mistake about how the doctrine operates.
questions.hint: Ask whether the shared facts are the ones that made the earlier rule sensible. Keep the inquiry on reasoning from material similarities.

questions.stem: This case: A judge comparing two disputes extends a rule to a new setting. The earlier rule had a clear rationale. Which proposition would a court most likely rely on in resolving this dispute?

options.text: Distinguishing is a rhetorical trick with no role in principled adjudication as this record presents them.
To distinguish a case is to declare the earlier judgment erroneous as this record presents them.
A case is distinguished when a factual difference undermines the reason that supported the earlier holding, so applying that holding would no longer make sense as this record presents them.
A single trivial factual difference always defeats a precedent as this record presents them.

questions.explanation: A good distinction targets the rationale. If the fact that changed is the one the earlier court relied on, the precedent does not govern; if it is incidental, the distinction should fail. Here the decisive point is distinguishing on material differences, so the result follows from that doctrine rather than from the surface appeal of a competing statement. Each distractor rests on a different mistake about how the doctrine operates.
questions.hint: Ask whether the changed fact was the reason for the earlier decision. Keep the inquiry on distinguishing on material differences.

questions.stem: The dispute: A judge comparing two disputes extends a rule to a new setting. The earlier rule had a clear rationale. Identify the statement that accurately reflects the applicable doctrine.

options.text: A judge may adopt a rule for one case without caring whether it can be applied consistently later under the circumstances described.
A rule should be chosen purely by which outcome the judge prefers, regardless of its logical reach under the circumstances described.
options.misconception: treats consequences as the only test

options.text: A coherent rule can never have exceptions, even when a principled distinction warrants one under the circumstances described.
When extending a rule, a court considers whether the principle behind it supports a coherent line of cases rather than an arbitrary boundary under the circumstances described.

questions.explanation: Doctrine develops by justification. A rule extended to a new setting should rest on a reason that can be stated generally, otherwise the line between cases becomes an unexplained preference. Here the decisive point is testing a proposed rule by its consequences, so the result follows from that doctrine rather than from the surface appeal of a competing statement. Each distractor rests on a different mistake about how the doctrine operates.
questions.hint: Ask whether the reason given would also decide the neighboring cases. Keep the inquiry on testing a proposed rule by its consequences.

questions.stem: In brief: A judge comparing two disputes extends a rule to a new setting. The earlier rule had a clear rationale. Which of the following best describes the legal standard a court would apply?

options.text: A hypothetical tests whether a proposed rule relies on the right distinction by pushing the rule to cases that reveal its implications given the events just recounted.
A hypothetical has no legal value because it concerns facts that did not occur given the events just recounted.
A vivid hypothetical automatically establishes the legal rule advocated given the events just recounted.
A hypothetical is a form of factual proof that the court must accept given the events just recounted.

questions.explanation: Hypotheticals are tools of reasoning. By changing one fact at a time, they expose whether a rule tracks a principled difference or merely the outcome the advocate wants in the case at hand. Here the decisive point is the role of hypotheticals in legal argument, so the result follows from that doctrine rather than from the surface appeal of a competing statement. Each distractor rests on a different mistake about how the doctrine operates.
questions.hint: Use the hypothetical to isolate which fact is doing the work. Keep the inquiry on the role of hypotheticals in legal argument.
